note: Generated from passages retrieved from the design document, then checked against those same passages by the lore critic. Corrections and the drafts they replaced are in critique/critique_log.json.
method: The critic is given the generated items and the same retrieved passages the writer was given, and never the writer's reasoning. Corrections are applied by the orchestrator; the drafts they replaced are kept here as `before`.

barks.summary: Fifteen of eighteen barks are clean; three state the fiction slightly past what the passages say — the first launch's fuel, what release can undo after a stow, and what a loss actually costs.

issues.quote: you don't have the rest of your tank
issues.evidence: [2.5d] "The base ship reaches the floor of the band on a ballistic arc with 29.5% of its tank left and a 97-second EVA window (measured). It can technically circularise at the floor, but arrives with 0% left and nothing to deorbit on — so the arc is the first launch's route"
issues.why: The passage is explicit that the base ship does have the fuel to circularise at the floor — what it does not have is anything left to deorbit on. The line replaces the real reason with a fuel shortfall the document denies.

corrected.line: Arc it, kid. Circularising is the rest of your tank — you'd get up there with nothing left to bring her back down.

issues.quote: let something go, right hand button, and it drifts off clean
issues.evidence: [2.4a] "Stow at the hold (E) to bank it. The greed decision: every trip out costs jetpack fuel and every stowed piece is permanent mass for the ride down." [2.4b] "The greed decision is informed but never reversible in flight."
issues.why: The dial crosses into red at a stow, so the mass that tripped it is already banked. Release (RMB) acts on the tethered piece, not on the hold — telling the player to shed mass now offers an undo the passages say does not exist.

corrected.line: Red on the scale, kid. What's banked is banked, and that ride down is destructive — the next piece you get on the tether, right hand button, let it drift.

issues.quote: your haul's the only thing that's gone
issues.evidence: [1b] "Every loss resets the current run: the ship respawns on the pad, cash and upgrades persist, and only this run's haul and its turnaround cost are lost"
issues.why: The document names two costs on a loss, the haul and the turnaround. Calling the haul the only loss understates the bill, and the bill is the register this game teaches failure in.

corrected.line: Suit was never rated for that, kid. She's back on the pad — you're out the haul and the cost of turning her around, and nothing past that.

recheck.summary: All three lines stay inside their passages — the arc-vs-circularise trade, the red zone's destructive verdict and RMB release, and the loss reset's haul-plus-turnaround cost are each stated as the document states them.

debris.summary: Twenty-one items pass; four need work — the reentry cone claims superlatives the passages hand to Armstrong's module, the antenna dish invents slot economy §4.3 rules out, the camera mast sells a degraded piece, and the wing spine quantifies a fuel cost nothing supports.

issues.quote: still wider than your cockpit
issues.evidence: [4.3] "Size classes, fragile flag, compactor, crane magnet, oversized junk. All exist to serve the endgame. Every piece is one slot; the module is simply very heavy."
issues.why: Raising this once, on this item, as the representative: §4.3 lists size classes, the fragile flag and oversized junk as cut from scope, and the loot table still carries all three (this row is flagged oversized; six rows are flagged FRAGILE). The collision is between the document and the table, not inside the writing — the table is what the game will spawn, so every size and fragility read in this batch stands, including this one. Nothing to correct here; it is a finding about the two sources disagreeing.

issues.quote: and it eats the whole slot doing it
issues.evidence: [4.3] "Every piece is one slot; the module is simply very heavy."
issues.why: This goes past the table's size class into cargo-slot economy. The table says oversized; it does not say oversized pieces consume capacity differently, and §4.3 positively states every piece is one slot — including this one. Bulk is fair to describe; a slot cost is not.

corrected.flavour: Folded in on itself like a dropped umbrella and still wider than your cockpit. It hangs where the scrap is cheap, and it is all elbows on the tether the whole way down.

issues.quote: or you'll be selling gravel from the bargain end of the band
issues.evidence: [5d] "Satellite → Apollo-era module that degrades (pristine → damaged → scrap) instead of being destroyed, and its condition selects the ending and scales payout."
issues.why: Selling the broken piece at a reduced rate is a payout that scales with condition. The passages define that mechanic for Armstrong's module alone, and define it by contrast — the module degrades *instead of being destroyed*, which is what ordinary debris does. A fragile piece may read as delicate and may be lost; it may not have a damaged resale price.

corrected.flavour: The optics head went first and the mast is holding its pieces together out of habit. Snatch it on the tether and there is nothing left to bring down — and this low, there was never much to bring down anyway.

issues.quote: it takes most of a tank to bring home
issues.evidence: [2.6a] "a ballistic arc never pays for circularisation, which is most of the delta-v, but it comes back in faster and hotter and gives a short working window; circularising costs the rest of the tank and buys time."
issues.why: The only tank arithmetic the passages give is routing: circularisation is most of the delta-v and costs the rest of the tank. Nothing in the passages or the table prices a single piece of cargo in fuel, so "most of a tank" is a quantity neither source supports. §2.6a does back the qualitative version — the good stuff "fights you on the tether and on the way down."

corrected.flavour: The full backbone of an array wing, panels stripped, still longer than your ship. It comes off the rich end of the band and it fights you on the tether and the whole way down.

issues.quote: The heaviest thing on the board, the highest hanging
issues.evidence: [2.6a] "At the very top hangs Armstrong's module: Apollo-era hardware that predates — and outlived — the cascade." / [4.3] "Every piece is one slot; the module is simply very heavy."
issues.why: Both superlatives belong to Armstrong's module. The table does settle superlatives among its own rows — 1600 kg at 276,000 m is the heaviest and highest row it carries — but the passages put the module above everything in the band and describe it as very heavy, so "the highest hanging" and "the heaviest thing on the board" are claims about the field, and the field has the module in it. This also steps on the module's whole job: the glint overhead that the player is not ready for yet.

corrected.flavour: Something big came down wearing this once and it is charred through, the ablative crumbling wherever you grip. The heaviest thing you can get a tether on short of the module itself, and the one most likely to come apart on the way to the deck.

recheck.summary: Two items go past what the sources support — one describes the tether destroying a fragile piece, one ranks it as the most fragile of the set — and the loot table's size and fragile fields collide with §4.3, which cuts both.

issues.quote: Snatch it on the tether and there is nothing left to bring down
issues.evidence: [4.3] "Size classes, fragile flag, compactor, crane magnet, oversized junk. All exist to serve the endgame. Every piece is one slot; the module is simply very heavy."
issues.why: The line does not just read as delicate — it states the outcome of grabbing it: the piece is gone the moment the tether takes it. No passage defines what the fragile flag does, so destruction-on-grab is a rule the writing invented. It also makes the piece unhaulable, which sits badly against the value-scales-with-mass haul the band is built on.

issues.quote: medium
issues.evidence: [4.3] "Size classes, fragile flag, compactor, crane magnet, oversized junk. All exist to serve the endgame. Every piece is one slot; the module is simply very heavy." — the loot table nonetheless ships "shattered_camera_mast 157 kg | 118,000 m (bottom third) | medium | FRAGILE", and carries size classes and fragile flags on rows throughout.
issues.why: Raised once for the whole set, on this item as representative. The collision is between the document and the data file, not inside the writing: §4.3 records size classes and the fragile flag as cut from scope, and the table the game will load still carries both. The fiction stays as written where it matches the table — the flag is what the game will spawn — but the two files need reconciling.

corrected.flavour: The optics head went first and the mast is holding its pieces together out of habit. Handle it gentle on the tether — and this low on the band, it is not worth much even whole.

issues.quote: the one most likely to come apart on the way to the deck
issues.evidence: The loot table carries FRAGILE as a boolean on seven rows — "cracked_solar_array ... FRAGILE", "shattered_camera_mast ... FRAGILE", "torn_radiator_panel ... FRAGILE", "optics_bench ... FRAGILE", "cracked_pressure_dome ... FRAGILE", "telescope_mirror_segment ... FRAGILE", "scorched_reentry_cone ... FRAGILE" — with no per-piece degree.
issues.why: The superlative claims a ranking that neither the passages nor the table contain: fragility is a flag, not a scale, and six other rows carry the same flag. The neighbouring superlative in this line — heaviest short of the module — is fine, because 1600 kg is the top row of the table and §4.3 puts the module above it.

corrected.flavour: Something big came down wearing this once and it is charred through, the ablative crumbling wherever you grip. The heaviest thing you can get a tether on short of the module itself, and it comes off the top of the band already half ruined.

postmortems.summary: Seven of nine screens hold; the (d) screen is titled STRANDED when the document resolves that clause as 0 HP, the refused screen plays Armstrong's fury as patience, and the stranded (c) screen asserts a descent the detector does not require.

issues.quote: Not like that, kid. She goes back up and you fly it again.
issues.evidence: [1b] "or refused — the module delivered in scrap state, Armstrong's fury (finale only, §2.6)"
issues.why: The document names this ending's reaction specifically — Armstrong's fury — and it is the finale beat the graded endings pay off. The line as written is patient and forgiving, which is the register of a teaching turnaround, not of the one delivery he refuses.

corrected.armstrong: Scrap. You hauled me back scrap, kid. She goes up again and you don't bring her down like that twice.

issues.quote: The descent stayed under the heat-speed threshold, so it was survivable.
issues.evidence: [2.7a] "An uncrewed ship grounding is a non-event — the ship parks inert and the run continues until the astronaut resolves it: board the parked ship → Landed; touch terrain not aboard → stranded."
issues.why: The detector is touching terrain while not aboard, full stop. A slow descent through the interface is only one route in; the other is an astronaut already on the ground beside a parked, uncrewed hull, who never fell through anything. The screen would state a cause that did not happen.

corrected.cause: The astronaut touched terrain while not aboard the ship. How you got there does not change it — a slow fall that never got hot, or a step away from a hull parked on the ground. Landed needs the pilot aboard.

issues.quote: STRANDED
issues.evidence: [2.7b] "(d) ship staged, chute shredded, on a descent whose minimum achievable touchdown speed exceeds the destruction cap — a conservative closed-form check, like the lamps — resolved immediately as 0 HP rather than flown out in real time."
issues.why: Clause (d) is a branch of the unwinnability check, but the document says it resolves as 0 HP, not as stranded. Since every reachable end state resolves to exactly one outcome (§2.7), a screen headed STRANDED names the wrong one — and the item's own rule_broken already says the check resolves it as 0 HP, so the screen contradicts itself as well as the passage.

corrected.title: SHIP DESTROYED
corrected.cause: Staged, chute shredded, and the lowest touchdown speed still reachable was past the destruction cap. The check called it there rather than making you fly the fall out.

recheck.summary: All three post-mortems hold against the passages — outcome, detector and register are right in each, including the correct call to title stranded_d as SHIP DESTROYED per §2.7's 0 HP resolution; one non-blocking bookkeeping note: stranded_d's grounded_in cites 2.2g for the shred rule, which is stated in 2.2f ("a parachute deployed during plasma shreds"), 2.2g covering only the post-plasma deploy order.
